lines: Picture a build system with ten thousand targets, each one depending on a handful of others.
Every target has to run after everything it needs — and that order isn't found by trial and error.
It falls straight out of the same two traversals already built this chapter, just pointed at how many things still have to finish first, instead of how far away something is.
Here's a graph with a cycle in it.
Can a graph like that have any valid order at all — one where everything comes after everything it depends on?
answer: No. A cycle rules it out completely.

Any order you tried would have to put some vertex in that cycle both before and after another vertex in the same cycle, since every vertex in a cycle can reach every other one in it. Nothing satisfies that — not a short cycle, not a long one.

lines: Here's the first way to find that order: keep a queue of every vertex that currently has nothing left pointing into it.
Pull one out, and for everything it points to, take away one incoming edge.

The moment one of those drops to zero, it joins the queue too. That's the exact same queue mechanics already built for the widening frontier — just counting down incoming edges instead of counting up distance.
Here's the second way: run the same depth-first search already built, and just write down the order things finished in.
Reverse that list, and you already have a valid order.
It doesn't have to match the queue's order vertex for vertex. It only has to respect every single edge — and it does.
Now run the queue version on a graph that actually has a cycle in it.
It drains itself dry. Some vertices never once hit zero, because they're all still waiting on each other.
The depth-first version doesn't need a separate check either — its own back-edge test already caught this the first time it ran.
Swap that plain queue for a heap that always pops the smallest label currently available.
Compared to the plain queue, on the same graph: always the identical order, always different, or could either happen?
answer: Either — and whenever they differ, the heap gives the smaller one.

A queue only remembers who arrived first. If a smaller-labelled vertex becomes available one round later, it still has to wait behind whoever got there before it. A heap breaks that tie by label, every single time.

lines: An order like this only says which things can come before which.
It says nothing about which vertices can reach each other at all, once cycles are allowed back in — whole groups that can each reach every other member of the group, and nothing outside it.
